title: Nan with Kids: 3-Day Family Plan — Temples, Rice-View Cafes, Bo Kluea | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A relaxed 3-day, 2-night Nan itinerary for families with kids: old-town temples, rice-field cafes in Pua, and the mountain salt wells at Bo Kluea — paced so kids don't burn out, with notes on driving, toilets, and food.
keywords: Nan with kids, Nan family travel, 3-day Nan itinerary, Pua rice-field cafe, Bo Kluea Nan
h1:
Nan with the Family
Temples · Rice-View Cafes · Bo Kluea in 3 Days
intro: Nan is easier to travel with kids than you'd expect. Distances in town are short, the temples are just a few steps apart, most cafes have wide open lawns where kids can run around, and the countryside near Pua and Bo Kluea isn't too rough if you pace it right. This plan runs 3 days and 2 nights: the old town on day one, the rice-field views of Pua on day two, then the mountain salt wells and a waterfall on the last day — built around plenty of rest, not a packed schedule.

blocks.html: With kids, the first thing to sort out is the car and the distances, because Nan's main sights are spread across several districts. Nan town to Pua is about 60 km, and Pua up to Bo Kluea is another 50 km or so of winding mountain road. If you have a little one who gets carsick easily, bring medicine and take breaks along the way. That's why this plan keeps day one easy and in-town, then eases out of the city over the following days.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Nan Old Town: Temple Walks and Local Bites

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: In Nan Town: Short Walks, Plenty of Rest

items.activity: Start at Wat Phumin to see the famous "Pu Man Ya Man" murals (the whispering-lovers painting)
items.note: The temple sits in the centre of town with a wide courtyard, strollers can get in, and there's no entry fee — just dress modestly

items.activity: Cross the road to the Nan National Museum to see the city's famous black elephant tusk
items.note: Adult entry is around 30 THB, kids free, and there's a lawn out front for kids to run around. Closed Monday–Tuesday

items.activity: Stop by Wat Ming Muang to see the all-white stucco-laced viharn — an easy photo spot near the museum
items.note: A few minutes' walk from the museum, so it's easy to wrap up the morning here

items.activity: Lunch at a northern-Thai restaurant in town — order khao soi, nam phrik num and crispy pork crackling for the kids to try
items.note: Pick a place with indoor seating; Nan afternoons get hot

items.activity: Back to the hotel in the afternoon to let the kids nap, then head out again later
items.note: Don't force the kids through the afternoon heat; a rest break makes the evening run smoother

items.activity: Walk the Kad Khuang Mueang Nan walking street (Friday–Sunday only) and sample the street snacks
items.note: If it's not a market day, go for an iced coffee along the Nan River instead — nice and chill

blocks.title: Day 1 Tip
blocks.html: Nan's in-town temples are clustered very close together — you can walk to almost all of them, so there's no need to drive around hunting for parking. If the kids are too tired to walk, renting a bicycle or a pedal trishaw around the old town is fun too.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Pua: Rice-View Cafes and a Hilltop Temple

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Out to Pua for Rice Fields and Mountains

items.activity: Leave Nan town for Pua district, about 60 km, roughly an hour's drive
items.note: The road is fairly smooth and not too steep, manageable for little ones, with petrol-station toilet stops along the way

items.activity: Ban Tai Lue Coffee — a hut-by-the-rice-field cafe with views of paddy fields and mountains
items.note: There's a wooden walkway out into the field for kids to wander; coffee starts around 40–60 THB, there are drinks for kids, and the Tai Lue atmosphere is the real thing

items.activity: Head up to Wat Phuket, a hilltop temple looking out over wide rice fields with Doi Phu Kha behind
items.note: There's a fish pond where kids can feed the fish, and the viewpoint photographs beautifully — mornings are clearer than afternoons

items.activity: Lunch at a restaurant in Pua — try local rice dishes or noodles
items.note: Pua has lots of small eateries; pick one with non-spicy options for the kids

items.activity: Stroll the Tai Lue community of Ban Nong Bua and see the flowing-water weave patterns
items.note: A gentle activity — kids get to watch real weavers at work, and you can buy woven cloth as a souvenir

items.activity: Check in to a stay around Pua, relax, and get ready to head up to Bo Kluea the next morning
items.note: Many Pua stays have rice-field views; in the cool season you'll wake up to mist

blocks.html: Pua is the part of a Nan trip families tend to love most, because it's nature without the hiking — you step out of the car and the rice-field view is right there. Most cafes have plenty of open space for kids to run, not cramped little shops, and the air stays cool and pleasant almost year-round.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Mountain Salt Wells and Sapan Waterfall

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Up to Bo Kluea, a Waterfall Stop, Then Loop Back

items.activity: Leave Pua for Bo Kluea district, about 50 km on winding mountain road
items.note: This stretch has lots of bends — if your kid gets carsick easily, give medicine before setting off, drive slowly, and pull over for breaks

items.activity: Visit the Bo Kluea Sinthao salt wells, mountain wells where salt is still boiled the traditional way
items.note: Entry is free, open roughly 07:00–18:00; kids get to see real salt-boiling, and you can buy spa salt as a souvenir

items.activity: Visit Sapan Waterfall or stop in Sapan village, ringed by mountains in a valley
items.note: Sapan Waterfall has water almost year-round and you can splash in the shallows — watch for slippery rocks and keep kids close

items.activity: Lunch at a cafe or eatery in Sapan, catching the cool breeze with a view
items.note: Spots up here cost a little more than in town because they're remote; coffee at some places starts around 80 THB

items.activity: Head back — either take the direct Bo Kluea–Nan town route, or loop along Route 1256 for the views
items.note: If the kids are tired, the direct route is shorter; save the Route 1256 sky-high road for next time

blocks.title: Driving with Kids in the Mountains
blocks.html: The Pua–Bo Kluea stretch is one continuous run of mountain bends. If your kid gets carsick easily, give the medicine at least half an hour before setting off, crack a window for fresh air, and pull over for a break every 30–40 minutes — don't drive it all in one go.

blocks.text: Getting Ready for a Family Trip to Nan

items: Best season — November to February brings cool air and beautiful mist, but it gets crowded and stays book up fast, so reserve ahead
Car — you really want your own car or a rental; public transport between districts is sparse and not convenient with kids
Medicine and essentials — motion-sickness pills, a basic first-aid kit, warm layers for the cool Bo Kluea mornings and evenings, and drinking water in the car
Toilets — easy to find in town and at the bigger cafes, but scarce on the Bo Kluea mountain road, so have the kids go before leaving each stop
Pacing — don't cram several districts into one day; once kids hit the wall they get cranky and the whole family wears out. Stick to one zone per day

blocks.text: If You Have Less Than 3 Days

items.name: 1 Day
items.blurb: Stay in Nan town — walk Wat Phumin, Wat Ming Muang and the museum, then sip a riverside coffee. Easy on the kids

items.name: 2 Days
items.blurb: Day one in town, day two out to Pua for the rice-field views and back; skip Bo Kluea if the kids are very young

items.name: 3 Days or More
items.blurb: You can do this full plan; add Doi Phu Kha or Route 1256 on the last day if the kids are up for it

faq.q: Is Nan tiring with young kids?
faq.a: Not if you stay in town, since the temples and cafes are close together and walkable. The part to watch is the road up to Bo Kluea, a long run of mountain bends — if your kid gets carsick easily, bring medicine and pull over for breaks along the way.

faq.q: Is Bo Kluea in Nan good for kids?
faq.a: Yes — entry is free and kids get to watch salt being boiled the traditional way for real. But the drive up is long and winding, so if your child is very young or gets carsick easily, you can drop it and just do the town and Pua.

faq.q: Do the rice-view cafes in Pua have space for kids to play?
faq.a: The bigger cafes like Ban Tai Lue Coffee have wide lawns and a walkway out into the rice field for kids to roam — they're not cramped little shops, so they're comfortable for families. Just don't let the kids wander down into the paddy itself.

faq.q: When should we visit Nan as a family?
faq.a: November through February is cool and pleasant with lovely mist, great for kids — but it's high season, so it gets crowded and stays fill up fast. Book several weeks ahead.

faq.q: Can you get around Nan town on your own without a car?
faq.a: Within the old town you can easily walk or cycle — the temples and museum are close together. But to reach Pua or Bo Kluea you'll need a car, since public transport between districts is sparse and not convenient with kids.
